title: “Vendepatria” and “Anti Vaccine”: Opinocracy and disinformation on WhatsApp in the 2023 constitutional process in Chile
screen_reason: Quantitative content analysis of political messages circulating in 214 public WhatsApp groups in Chile during the 2023 constitutional council campaign. Reports the share of coded messages classified as disinformation with explicit denominators (23% of 342 unique political messages; 19.4% vs 8.7% by group political orientation of 3,047 messages including repetitions), plus a falsity breakdown inside the disinformation set.

estimates.date: 8 March to 8 May 2023 (official campaign period for the constitutional council election)
estimates.measure_type: % of unique political messages circulating in public WhatsApp groups (those repeated more than four times) coded as disinformation
estimates.denominator: 342 unique political messages repeated more than four times, drawn from 64,965 messages posted by 3,874 users in 214 public WhatsApp groups
estimates.definition: Message coded into the inductive category 'Desinformación' by trained research assistants: a lax definition covering conspiracy theories, false content and unverifiable content (future projections, speculation) and other claims resting on uncheckable facts; opinion content is explicitly excluded
estimates.misinfo_def: “Desinformación: Definición laxa que incluye teorías conspirativas, contenido falso y contenido no verificable (como proyecciones de futuro, especulaciones) y otros apoyados en hechos no comprobables.” (‘Disinformation: a lax definition that includes conspiracy theories, false content and unverifiable content (such as future projections, speculation) and others resting on uncheckable facts.’)
estimates.source_quote: El tipo de contenido más frecuente fue opinión (N=108, 32% de los mensajes únicos), seguido por información (N=88, 26%), luego desinformación (N=78, 23%), movilización (N=28, 19%).
estimates.page_loc: p. 61, Section 4 Resultados y discusión; Figura 2
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Four trained research assistants coded messages with a codebook developed in earlier work; intercoder reliability 93% agreement (Krippendorff's alpha = 0.84) for whether a message referred to the plebiscite and 78% agreement (alpha = 0.69) for political content type. Disinformation items were then fact-checked by one co-author against official sources (laws, decrees, government and scientific reports) and alternative sources (media, civil-society reports, expert analysis).
estimates.moderator_quote: Para analizar con más detalle y poner el foco en el contenido que tuvo más difusión en la red, analizamos mensajes con más de cuatro repeticiones, resultando un total de 501 mensajes únicos, de los cuales 342 son mensajes únicos de carácter político (totalizando 2.694 incluyendo repeticiones).
estimates.notes: Headline prevalence figure. Denominator is truncated to messages repeated more than four times, hence denom_selection=curated (‘the threshold of four repetitions is relatively arbitrary’ per the authors, chosen to keep manual coding feasible). Internal inconsistency in the paper: the body text gives desinformación N=78 out of 342, while Figura 2 plots 77 with N=341; the body-text value is used here. The same sentence gives movilización as 'N=28, 19%', which cannot be a share of 342 and contradicts Figura 2 (58); that category is not extracted. English translation of source quote: 'The most frequent content type was opinion (N=108, 32% of unique messages), followed by information (N=88, 26%), then disinformation (N=78, 23%), mobilisation (N=28, 19%).' QUOTE NOTE: source_quote is the sentence as printed but with the PDF's line-break hyphenation closed up (the text file renders it 'se- guido' and 'desinfor- macion'); quote_verbatim=false records that it is faithful rather than byte-identical to the extracted text.

estimates.measure_type: % of political messages (including repetitions) in conservative WhatsApp groups coded as disinformation
estimates.denominator: 2,898 political messages (repetitions included) originating in the 81 conservative ('Rechazo') WhatsApp groups
estimates.definition: Same 'Desinformación' coding category, applied to political messages with four or more repetitions, counted with repetitions and split by the political orientation of the group of origin
estimates.misinfo_def: “Desinformación: Definición laxa que incluye teorías conspirativas, contenido falso y contenido no verificable…” (‘a lax definition that includes conspiracy theories, false content and unverifiable content…’)
estimates.source_quote: dos veces más presencia de desinformación que en los grupos progresistas (19,4% versus 8,7%).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Four trained research assistants, codebook from earlier work; alpha = 0.69 for the political content-type variable, alpha = 0.84 for plebiscite relevance; author fact-checking of the disinformation subset against official and alternative sources.
estimates.moderator_quote: Tabla 3: Contenido político detallado por categoría de análisis y orientación política del grupo de origen (N=3.047, incluyendo repeticiones).
estimates.notes: Kept as a subgroup row because the conservative/progressive asymmetry is the paper's stated hypothesis and headline finding, not an incidental demographic split. Denominator differs from row 1: this table counts messages WITH repetitions (3,047 total: 2,898 conservative, 149 progressive), while row 1 counts unique messages. Chi-square (1, N=3,047) = 9.85, p = 0.0017; Fisher exact odds ratio = 0.3973, p < 0.001. English translation: 'Additionally, as anticipated in the hypothesis, in conservative groups we detected twice as much disinformation as in progressive groups (19.4% versus 8.7%).'

estimates.denominator: 149 political messages (repetitions included) originating in the 133 progressive ('Apruebo') WhatsApp groups
estimates.definition: Same 'Desinformación' coding category, applied to political messages with four or more repetitions, counted with repetitions and split by the political orientation of the group of origin
estimates.misinfo_def: “Desinformación: Definición laxa que incluye teorías conspirativas, contenido falso y contenido no verificable…” (‘a lax definition that includes conspiracy theories, false content and unverifiable content…’)
estimates.source_quote: dos veces más presencia de desinformación que en los grupos progresistas (19,4% versus 8,7%).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Four trained research assistants, codebook from earlier work; alpha = 0.69 for the political content-type variable; author fact-checking of the disinformation subset against official and alternative sources.
estimates.moderator_quote: Tabla 3: Contenido político detallado por categoría de análisis y orientación política del grupo de origen (N=3.047, incluyendo repeticiones).
estimates.notes: Progressive counterpart to the conservative row; both are the paper's headline test. Very small denominator (149 messages, 13 disinformation), because progressive groups produced far fewer highly repeated political messages despite being two-thirds of the groups.

estimates.measure_type: % of NON-political unique messages (repeated more than four times) identified as disinformation
estimates.value_raw: 17% (“una frecuencia un poco más baja (17% versus 23%)”)
estimates.denominator: The non-political unique messages repeated more than four times (159 = 501 unique messages minus 342 political ones); the paper does not state this denominator explicitly
estimates.definition: Non-political messages, not fully coded into the six political categories, but screened for disinformation; these centred on COVID-19 and global warming
estimates.misinfo_def: “Desinformación: Definición laxa que incluye teorías conspirativas, contenido falso y contenido no verificable…”
estimates.n: approximately 159 non-political unique messages (denominator inferred, not stated)
estimates.source_quote: El resultado muestra una frecuencia un poco más baja (17% versus 23%)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same research-assistant coding team; the paper notes non-political content was not fully coded, only screened for disinformation, so reliability statistics for this subset are not reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: El contenido no político no fue codificado completamente, pues las categorías se refieren a contenido político, pero sí se identificó la desinformación.
estimates.notes: ADJUDICATOR: the 17% is verbatim but its denominator is never stated; 159 is inferred as 501 unique messages minus 342 political ones. Topic is mixed (COVID-19 plus climate), coded 'other'. Easy to drop if the review requires a stated denominator. English translation: 'Non-political content was not fully coded, since the categories refer to political content, but disinformation was identified. The result shows a slightly lower frequency (17% versus 23%) when the conversation moves away from politics, centring on messages about Covid-19 and global warming.'

estimates.measure_type: % of election-related disinformation messages fact-checked as outright 'false' (within the disinformation set only)
estimates.value_raw: 41% of N=37 disinformation messages (Falso 41%, Engañoso 32%, Inchequeable 27%)
estimates.denominator: 37 election-related messages already coded as disinformation and then fact-checked
estimates.definition: Fact-check verdict 'Falso': the information does not exist or there are data that totally contradict it, with no interpretations that refute the contradiction
estimates.misinfo_def: “Falso: La información no existe o hay datos que la contradicen totalmente.” (‘False: the information does not exist or there are data that totally contradict it.’)
estimates.source_quote: la proporción de información verificada como “falsa” es la más alta (41%)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: One co-author fact-checked each item with a four-step procedure: trace the origin/first appearance of the viral content; consult official sources (laws, decrees, government and scientific reports); consult alternative sources (media, civil-society reports, expert analysis); assign a verdict per Table 1 (Verdadero / Falso / Engañoso / Inchequeable). Direct contact with the original source was not possible because messages were anonymous.
estimates.moderator_quote: Tabla 1: Categorías de verificación — Falso: La información no existe o hay datos que la contradicen totalmente. No hay interpretaciones que la desmientan.
estimates.notes: R3 row: falsity computed INSIDE a misinformation-only sample, so within_misinfo_content=true (appendix only, not a prevalence estimate). Sets up the strict-definition variant of row 1: 41% of the 37 fact-checked election disinformation items were outright false, the remainder misleading (32%) or uncheckable (27%). The N=37 denominator is smaller than the 78 disinformation messages in row 1 because only the election-related subset was fact-checked. Engañoso (32%) and Inchequeable (27%) are verbatim too but not extracted as separate rows (R4).

missed_or_uncertain: 1) 'uno de cada tres mensajes únicos sobre el tema [voto nulo], tanto en grupos progresistas como conservadores, se basa en supuestos falsos o engañosos' ('one in three unique messages on the null-vote topic, in both progressive and conservative groups, rests on false or misleading assumptions') — no denominator count given, so no row (R8). 2) The Engañoso (32%) and Inchequeable (27%) verdict shares from Figura 5 are verbatim but are complements of the same 37-item base as the extracted 'Falso' row; not split out per R4. 3) Table 3 also gives conservative/progressive shares of the TOTAL for each category (e.g. disinformation 97.7% conservative / 2.3% progressive); these are a source-attribution split, not a prevalence share, so no row. 4) Figura 3 splits political content types into 'Elecciones' vs 'Político (no Elecciones)' but reports only a bar chart with no readable percentages in the extracted text. 5) CONSTRUCT JUDGEMENT CALL: the denominator is messages posted and forwarded into public WhatsApp groups, filtered to those repeated more than four times, and the paper frames the object as 'circulación'/'difusión' (circulation/spread). I coded SHARING (content_share) because a class of users is measured by what they forward and the repetition filter selects re-shared content. An adjudicator could defensibly code CONTENT if WhatsApp group messages are treated as items that simply exist on the platform. 6) The paper's disinformation category is deliberately lax (conspiracy theories, unverifiable speculation), broader than a fact-check-only definition; breadth coded 'misleading' throughout except the strict 'Falso' row.

rob.design: Convenience sample of 214 public WhatsApp groups located by searching public Facebook groups and open websites for links to groups whose names contained 'Apruebo' or 'Rechazo' and related to the Chilean constitutional processes; one author joined with a dedicated research account. 64,965 messages from 3,874 users captured 8 March to 8 May 2023. Analysis restricted to messages repeated more than four times (501 unique, 342 political, 2,694 with repetitions). Four trained research assistants coded independently with a codebook; intercoder agreement 93% (Krippendorff's alpha = 0.84) for plebiscite relevance and 78% (alpha = 0.69) for political content type, which the authors acknowledge is suboptimal but defend as acceptable for tentative conclusions. Disinformation items were then fact-checked by one co-author against official and alternative sources; no direct contact with original message sources was possible. The authors state the sample is not representative.
rob.item6_quote: 1. Desinformación: Definición laxa que incluye teorías conspirativas, contenido falso y contenido no verificable (como proyecciones de futuro, especulaciones) y otros apoyados en hechos no comprobables. No incluye contenido que refleja puntos de vista sin hechos, la expresión valórica o juicios sobre un tema, codificado como “Opinión” (ver ítem 4).
